articles.title: Amazon will pay $2.5 billion to settle the FTC’s Prime lawsuit
articles.summary: Amazon will pay $2.5 billion to settle a lawsuit from the FTC that claimed the company tricked people into signing up for Prime and made it difficult to cancel.
articles.body: Amazon has agreed to pay $2.5 billion to settle a lawsuit from the Federal Trade Commission, which claimed it tricked millions of customers into subscribing to Prime and made it hard to cancel. Under the agreement, Amazon will pay a $1 billion civil penalty, along with $1.5 billion that it will pay back to an estimated 35 million customers impacted by the company’s “deceptive” sign-up process. Amazon must also stop its “unlawful enrollment and cancellation practices” for Prime. A jury was originally set to decide the outcome of a lawsuit during a trial that began in Seattle this week, but now that’s been cut short by the settlement. The FTC filed its lawsuit against Amazon in 2023, accusing it of using “dark patterns” to deceive people into signing up for Prime. It also alleged Amazon executives were aware of these practices, and also made it “exceedingly difficult” for customers to cancel their Prime memberships by having them go through unnecessary steps. Now, the FTC will require Amazon to change its Prime signup process by having a “clear and conspicuous button” for customers to decline a Prime subscription. That means Amazon can no longer show customers a button that says, “No, I don’t want Free Shipping” to decline a Prime subscription. Additionally, Amazon must make it easier for Prime members to cancel their subscription, using the same steps they took to sign up. “The process cannot be difficult, costly, or time-consuming,” The FTC says. The ecommerce giant is also required to clearly describe Prime’s terms and conditions during the enrollment process, including its cost, auto-renewal policies, and cancellation procedures. ”Amazon and our executives have always followed the law and this settlement allows us to move forward and focus on innovating for customers,” Amazon says in a statement posted to its website. “We work incredibly hard to make it clear and simple for customers to both sign up or cancel their Prime membership, and to offer substantial value for our many millions of loyal Prime members around the world.” The settlement resolves one of the FTC’s legal cases against Amazon, as the agency has also filed an antitrust lawsuit against the company for allegedly punishing sellers who sell products for a lower price outside of its online marketplace. Amazon is expected to go to trial over this lawsuit in 2027. “The evidence showed that Amazon used sophisticated subscription traps designed to manipulate consumers into enrolling in Prime, and then made it exceedingly hard for consumers to end their subscription,” FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson said in a statement. Update, September 25th: Added a statement from Amazon.

articles.title: News Flash: 70% of Wall Street Institutions Are Calling for at Least a 50-Basis-Point Fed Rate Hike in 2026
articles.summary: Trumpflation and the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out are expected to force Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) int...
articles.body:
Today, Sept. 16, is the day all of Wall Street has been waiting for. In mere hours, at 2 p.m. ET, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will announce what, if any, monetary policy changes have been made to the federal funds target rate -- and that answer is expected to cause wild vacillations in the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI), S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC), and Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC).

Over the last few weeks, the odds of a Fed rate hike have hovered around 50-50, both on prediction markets and for the CME Group 's (NASDAQ:CME) proprietary FedWatch Tool. But there's been a decisive shift in expectations following the release of the August inflation report .

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

All eyes are on Fed Chair Warsh and the FOMC. Image source: Official Federal Reserve Photo.

Since Kevin Warsh became Fed chair nearly four months ago, he's instituted several reforms, none of which have gained more notoriety than removing forward-looking guidance from FOMC meeting statements. Unfortunately, this lack of transparency that the equity and bond markets had become accustomed to for more than two decades has made it considerably more challenging to decipher what the central bank will do next.

While a few Wall Street institutions and economists altered their take on the FOMC's Sept. 16 meeting after Warsh's Jackson Hole speech on Aug. 28, we witnessed a monstrous shift in thinking after the August inflation report was released.

According to calls aggregated by The Wall Street Journal and published on X (formerly Twitter) by Nick Timiraos, its chief economics correspondent, only four of 20 institutions don't expect a rate hike this year, and 14 of the 16 that do are calling for a 50- or 75-basis-point increase to the federal funds target rate in 2026.

As a reminder, the last time the Fed kicked off a rate-hiking cycle with a 50-basis-point increase was in March 2022, which was followed by a 13% decline in the benchmark S&P 500 over the next three months.

Trumpflation and the AI revolution may force the Fed into action

Although a rate hike is bound to draw the ire of President Donald Trump, who's been advocating for lower interest rates since his second term began, Warsh and the FOMC may have little choice if they want to deliver price stability.

articles.title: SEC unveils exemption for tokenized stock trading
articles.summary: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) unveiled its long-awaited “innovation exemption” Thursday, a new order aimed at clearing the way for tokenized stock trading in the U.S. The order creates a pair of five-year exemptions. The first exempts platforms that host tokenized stock trading from the commission’s definition of an exchange, while the second exempts…
articles.body:
The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) unveiled its long-awaited “innovation exemption” Thursday, a new order aimed at clearing the way for tokenized stock trading in the U.S.

The order creates a pair of five-year exemptions. The first exempts platforms that host tokenized stock trading from the commission’s definition of an exchange, while the second exempts liquidity providers in the space from its definition of a dealer.

“Over the past several years, advancements in distributed ledger technology have facilitated innovations in trading across non-security crypto assets,” the SEC noted in a fact sheet.

However, it suggested that tokenized stock trading platforms “may face substantial challenges with complying with the Federal securities laws without potentially burdensome changes to its business model.”

Tokenized stocks are digital versions of real-world stocks. They are represented by digital tokens on the blockchain, the technology that forms the foundation of cryptocurrency.

The SEC’s innovation exemption specifically applies to platforms that rely on automated market makers, which are often used by decentralized crypto exchanges.

Traditional market makers are separate financial institutions or individuals that provide liquidity for a market. Automated market makers, by contrast, depend on liquidity pools supplied by users and rely on an algorithm to automatically set prices.

To fall under the SEC’s exemption, these platforms have to be permissioned. Permissioned blockchains require some standards for people to access and trade on them, unlike public blockchains that are open to anyone.

Holders of the tokenized stock must also have the “same rights and privileges” as a traditional stock of an “equivalent class,” the SEC noted.

The new order comes just two days after the Clarity Act came up short in the Senate. The crypto regulation bill failed to secure enough support to clear a procedural hurdle on the Senate floor.

SEC Chair Paul Atkins hinted at the agency’s plans Wednesday.

“I have been unequivocal: with or without legislation, we will act decisively within the SEC’s statutory authority to deliver certainty for American investors and for the entrepreneurs shaping our technological future,” he wrote on the social platform X. “Stay tuned.”

images.caption: FILE – The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission building is shown in Washington on Aug. 5, 2017. (AP Andrew Harnik, File)

articles.title: Trump administration allows truck drivers hauling gas, diesel to work longer hours
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced Wednesday the Trump administration will temporarily increase how long gas and diesel truck drivers can drive, as fuel costs remain elevated amid the Iran war. Under the 90-day waiver from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), truck drivers hauling gasoline and diesel can drive for up to 16 hours…
articles.body:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced Wednesday the Trump administration will temporarily increase how long gas and diesel truck drivers can drive, as fuel costs remain elevated amid the Iran war .

Under the 90-day waiver from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), truck drivers hauling gasoline and diesel can drive for up to 16 hours within a 24-hour window — an increase from the 14-hour limit under normal conditions. The waiver took effect Wednesday and expires on Dec. 16.

Drivers must still take a minimum of one six-hour break in their truck’s sleeper berth during the 24-hour period. If their vehicle does not have a separate bed area, the driver must take at least an eight-hour break during the aforementioned window.

The waiver applies to truck drivers “in good standing” and excludes “anyone with a conditional safety rating or an active out-of-service order,” the Transportation Department noted in a release .

“From unleashing American energy production to alleviating short-term supply chain pressures, the Trump Administration is constantly taking action to lower fuel prices,” Duffy wrote. “Our great American truckers will continue to haul the products that power America and keep our economy moving.”

The FMCSA waiver requires motor carriers to provide drivers with at least 10 consecutive hours of rest if they need it immediately. Motor carriers must also notify the agency within two business days of a crash.

Gas prices remain at more than $4 per gallon on average, as the war in Iran approaches the seven-month mark. The Islamic Republic’s restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have hamstrung the global oil trade , with prices in the U.S. impacted despite it being a net exporter of oil .

The national average price of a gallon of regular gas is roughly $4.44 as of Thursday, up from roughly $4.28 a week ago and $1.50 higher than two days before the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran war, according to data from AAA .

Diesel in the U.S. also costs roughly $6.40 per gallon as of Thursday, with Californians seeing a price of about $8.35 per gallon on average, AAA reported.

President Trump on Wednesday reiterated his view that higher gas prices are worth enduring to ensure Iran cannot develop a nuclear weapon.

“It’s a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done, remember that,” Trump said in North Carolina while stumping for GOP Senate candidate Michael Whatley.

The president also predicted fuel prices will “come tumbling down” once the conflict ends, which he said last week will occur after November’s midterms .

images.caption: A truck carrying fuel is seen parked at a gas station, April 14, 2026, in Dallas.

articles.title: Kaepernick: Van Jones tried to broker a meeting between Trump, former QB
articles.summary: Former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick revealed Wednesday that CNN analyst and former Obama administration adviser Van Jones attempted to broker a meeting between the football player and President Trump. Appearing on a MediasTouch podcast, host Ben Meiselas asked Kaepernick about a “Black Summit” the former San Francisco 49ers quarterback was invited to during Trump’s first…
articles.body:
Former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick revealed Wednesday that CNN analyst and former Obama administration adviser Van Jones attempted to broker a meeting between the football player and President Trump.

Appearing on a MediasTouch podcast , host Ben Meiselas asked Kaepernick about a “Black Summit” the former San Francisco 49ers quarterback was invited to during Trump’s first term.

“What I’ve learned over the years is there is going to be a constant attempt to be able to co-opt people who are trying to work for the benefit of the people, and what we saw in this moment was, you know, part of that conversation,” Kaepernick said about the event. “What was relayed to me was the outreach came from Van Jones for this.”

“I don’t know the details around it because, candidly, as soon as it came up as, ‘Hey, here is the opportunity,’ it was immediately rejected,” he continued.

The president’s relationship with Kaepernick throughout his first term was complicated as Trump criticized the quarterback for kneeling on the field during the national anthem in protest of racial injustice.

“But I will tell you — you cannot disrespect our country, our flag, our anthem, you cannot do that,” Trump said at the time.

Trump also stated he would support the NFL suspending Kaepernick indefinitely because of his protest.

Kaepernick said Trump’s actions made him think the invite to the summit was “a facade that he’s working for Black people or trying to be in the benefit of Black people,” but “history shows otherwise.”

“This is after him going out publicly and trying to target me in my employment,” he added.

Kaepernick specifically called out connections between Trump and the Reform Alliance — where Jones formerly served as CEO — saying, “Ultimately, what we see is on the other side of that, you know, pardons being handed out, and we’re seeing those pay-for-play right now.”

Kaepernick has been out of the NFL since March 2017, when he opted out of his 49ers contract, though he has not officially retired. He filed a grievance at the time that accused NFL owners of colluding to keep him from playing.

The lawsuit named Trump and former Vice President Mike Pence as a “colluding force” to prevent him from signing a contract within the league. The case was reportedly settled in 2019 for less than $10 million.

In the same year, Trump said he would “love” to see Kaepernick back in the league, noting that NFL owners would sign him “if he was good enough.”

images.caption: Colin Kaepernick arrives for a workout for NFL scouts and media on Nov. 16, 2019, in Riverdale, Ga.

articles.title: Oral pill could provide new option for people with sleep apnea
articles.summary: Around 30 million people in the U.S. suffer from the disease, according to the American Lung Association, but millions go undiagnosed.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — An oral drug designed to treat sleep apnea showed promising results in a recent clinical trial, suggesting there may be another alternative on the market soon for people who don’t like using Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) machines.

In the phase 3 trial, 646 adults with mild to severe obstructive sleep apnea were given the once-nightly pill AD109, Science Daily reported , based on materials provided by the American Thoracic Society. Researchers found that more than 40 percent of participants’ conditions improved to a less severe OSA classification, while 18 percent achieved complete control of the disease.

The trial also found that the number of breathing interruptions fell by 44 percent in patients who took the medication, while the placebo group only showed a less than 20 percent reduction, according to Science Daily. The outlet said AD109 is intended to work by supporting throat muscles, “so the airway is less likely to sag or collapse during sleep.”

Obstructive sleep apnea is a breathing disorder that occurs when the throat muscles relax and repeatedly block the airway during sleep. It affects nearly one billion adults worldwide and is linked to serious health problems, including heart disease and stroke.

Around 30 million people in the U.S. suffer from the disease, according to the American Lung Association , but millions go undiagnosed and untreated.

For those who are diagnosed, CPAP machines are the most common treatment ; however, some people cannot tolerate them or decline to use them. The participants in the study, which was published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine, all fit into one of those categories, per Science Daily.

It is important to note that while side effects were described as “mild and expected,” 21 percent of patients in the study stopped taking the drug because of them, the outlet added. Still, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has given AD109 the Fast Track designation, “reflecting the need for effective and well-tolerated drug therapies for the condition.”

NewsNation recently reported on a review published in JAMA Otolaryngology that found GLP-1 drugs may reduce the severity of obesity-related sleep apnea.

NewsNation staff contributed to this report.
tags: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine

images.caption: FILE – A woman demonstrates how she puts on her sleep apnea breathing device at her home in Los Angeles Thursday, July 12, 2018. Tirzepatide, used to treat diabetes and obesity, can help with sleep apnea, a dangerous disorder in which people struggle to breathe while they sleep, according to a study, published Friday, June 21, 2024, in the New England Journal of Medicine, (AP Photo/Reed Saxon, File)

articles.title: Kim introduces bill to eliminate long waiting periods for disability benefits
articles.summary: Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) on Thursday introduced legislation to phase out waiting periods for Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) and Medicare benefits. Kim’s bill, the Stop the Wait Act, would phase out the five-month waiting period for SSDI benefits over five years as well as eliminate the 24-month waiting period for Medicare disability benefits. The…
articles.body:
Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) on Thursday introduced legislation to phase out waiting periods for Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) and Medicare benefits.

Kim’s bill, the Stop the Wait Act, would phase out the five-month waiting period for SSDI benefits over five years as well as eliminate the 24-month waiting period for Medicare disability benefits.

The senator from New Jersey cited data from the Government Accountability Office that found more than 100,000 people died between fiscal 2008 and 2019 while waiting for a final decision on their SSDI benefits. This figure represents roughly 1.2 percent of total disability applicants who filed an appeal.

“It is horrifying that any American should be forced to endure months or even years of waiting for benefits they worked hard to earn. Care cannot be put on hold. Congress needs to step up for our disability community and end these harmful waiting periods once and for all,” Kim said in a statement.

A similar bill with the same title was introduced last February by Democratic Rep. Lloyd Doggett (Texas), but it did not progress after being referred to the House Ways and Means Committee.

SSDI benefits are paid to people who are unable to work because of a medical condition that is expected to last at least on year or potentially result in death. Diseases of the musculoskeletal system and connective tissue are by far the most common conditions reported among SSDI beneficiaries, accounting for roughly 65 percent, according to a 2024 report from the Social Security Administration.

In a statement, Kim’s office argued that Congress had already moved to eliminate waiting periods for certain situations, such as for people with ALS.

The bill has been endorsed by the Federation of American Hospitals, American Association of People with Disabilities, the Alzheimer’s Association, Pandemic Patients and the National Alliance on Mental Illness, among others.

images.caption: Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) addresses reporters outside the Senate Chamber on July 22, 2026, to discuss Senate Democrats’ efforts to prevent President Trump from subverting the midterm elections in the fall.

articles.title: Your robotaxi might be a narc
articles.summary: Waymo called the cops on two passengers after detecting a gun in the vehicle. The incident raises questions about the limits of privacy inside an autonomous vehicle.
articles.body: In early September, two teenagers got into a Waymo, but then ended up in the back of a police car. The robotaxi company said it detected “a violation of our terms of service involving a firearm,” pulled the car over, and alerted emergency services, according to the Los Angeles Times. Police arrested the passengers after allegedly finding a loaded AR-style “ghost gun” in the vehicle. The arrests exposed a lot of unanswered questions about privacy and autonomous vehicles, including what they are recording, what they do with the footage, and how much privacy riders should expect while riding inside them. Waymo’s camera-covered cars have already been drawn into the debate over privacy and surveillance. On a number of occasions, law enforcement agencies have obtained search warrants for footage captured by its cars, according to Bloomberg. Last year, the LAPD obtained footage of a hit-and-run that was recorded by a nearby Waymo vehicle. During anti-ICE protests in Los Angeles, five Waymos were vandalized and set on fire amid questions about whether the vehicles could be capturing images of protesters that might be used as evidence to identify or arrest them. Waymo does not publicly disclose how many law enforcement requests it receives or how often it complies. Those concerns echo the backlash against Flock’s network of automated license-plate readers, which have given police the ability to track cars across jurisdictions and have prompted growing fears about government surveillance and misuse. Unlike fixed Flock cameras, Waymos move through cities carrying cameras both outside and inside their vehicles. [Image: Waymo Ojai autonomous robotaxi travels through the Fourth and Howard streets intersection outside Moscone West, which displays banners for the 2026 Pokemon World Championships, San Francisco, California, August 20, 2026. The latest case of the arrested teens takes those concerns a step further. Police did not approach Waymo after a crime looking for footage its cameras happened to capture. Waymo detected something inside the car and initiated the police response itself. Waymo spokesperson Julia Ilina told The Verge in an email that the company uses its internal cameras to help enforce its terms of service, including detecting prohibited items and behavior. She said it uses automated technology to help Waymo’s teams identify potential violations, such as the presence of firearms inside the vehicle. “If Waymo detects a firearm in the vehicle, we may reach out to local law enforcement,” she added. Waymo did not explain how its automated system determines whether something may be a firearm, how confident it has to be before something gets flagged, what role humans play between an automated alert and a call to police, or what other violations of its terms of service might prompt a police response. Those are important omissions. This wasn’t a human taxi driver deciding to call 911. It was a driverless car, equipped with cameras and an AI brain, escalating a situation involving its passengers to police. Bob Somers, a former engineer at autonomous vehicle company Zoox and technical adviser to the AV-safety nonprofit SAVE-US, said he would expect Waymo’s system to look for a range of potentially dangerous weapons and behaviors. The software may not need to decide with certainty that it has seen a firearm. It could instead flag something that resembles one for further review, he said. “If there is a certain set of objects detected, then that would probably loop in a remote operator to take a look at what’s going on,” Somers said. Phil Koopman, a Carnegie Mellon University professor emeritus who researches autonomous vehicle safety, said computer vision systems can be trained to recognize objects and potentially dangerous situations. "“If there is a certain set of objects detected, then that would probably loop in a remote operator to take a look at what’s going on.”" - Bob Somers “If you can train a computer to look at the road and decide how to drive, you can train a computer to decide if somebody’s holding a gun,” Koopman said. But, he added, those systems are “never 100 percent accurate.” That’s where the unanswered question about human review becomes important. A human taxi driver who sees a passenger holding something has context. They’ve been in the car for the entire ride. They can hear what the passengers are saying and ask questions. They can decide whether the object is a real gun, a toy, or something else entirely. Back in July, Waymo reported two teens to the police for underage drinking and shooting a toy gun loaded with water beads from the vehicle. It was not clear whether the teens ultimately faced any charges. A remote worker brought in to review a flagged moment might not have all of that context because they haven’t experienced the entire ride the way a human driver would. Waymo says its interior microphones are generally active only during calls with Rider Support or when riders enable them, meaning a reviewer may not be able to hear what preceded the flagged moment. As of earlier this year, Waymo has about 70 “remote assistance agents” on duty at a given time in the US and the Philippines, who “provide advice and support to the Waymo Driver but do not directly control, steer, or drive the vehicle.” Waymo has not said whether the people reviewing possible violations inside its cars are among those agents. “It’s really important that Waymo gets it right when they alert the police to something dangerous,” Koopman said. Beyond undermining riders’ trust in robotaxis, a false alarm could put passengers at risk during a police encounter. Then there’s the question of what Waymo tells riders to expect. Without a driver in the front seat, robotaxis can feel more private than they actually are. In 2023, the San Francisco Standard spoke with four people who said they had hooked up or had sex in Cruise robotaxis, despite the cameras inside them. The publication could not find anyone who said they had done so in a Waymo, but the episodes illustrate how readily passengers can mistake the absence of a human driver for the absence of a witness. Waymo’s terms of service requires riders to comply with applicable laws and prohibits them from creating a dangerous condition, carrying weapons “or anything that resembles a weapon, e.g. toy gun,” or using drugs. Riders must be at least 18 to ride alone in San Francisco. The two riders arrested this month allegedly violated both the age and weapons restrictions. The terms say Waymo can suspend or terminate a rider’s access if it believes the rider has violated the rules. Earlier this year, Waymo suspended the account used to book a ride after three boys were photographed hanging out the windows of the vehicle and taking selfies. But they do not plainly tell passengers that the company may call the police based on what it sees inside the car. "“It’s really important that Waymo gets it right when they alert the police to something dangerous.”" - Phil Koopman Waymo’s public camera policy says its interior cameras can be used to “check that in-car rules are being followed” and “promote safety and security.” It says Waymo Support may review recorded video after an issue is brought to the company’s attention and, in urgent circumstances, access live video during a trip. The policy also says Waymo may share certain data with law enforcement as needed to comply with legal requirements, enforce agreements, or protect the safety of riders and others. But it doesn’t specify that automated monitoring inside the vehicle may trigger Waymo itself to contact police. Hayley Tsukayama, director of state affairs at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, called Waymo’s public policies “very broad.” Riders shouldn’t have to infer from language about “safety and security” that their behavior could result in a police response, she said, adding that Waymo should clearly disclose that possibility before passengers get into the car. “I’m not condoning illegal behavior in rideshares,” she said, but “if they’re going to share it with authorities, then that should be clearly stated in the policy.” As it stands, Tsukayama said, “it is outside of the expectations of consumers.” Then again, robotaxis themselves are outside the norm. As they become more common, riders may have to develop a new set of expectations about what happens inside them. A human driver can decide how to respond to what happens in their car. In a robotaxi, cameras and software can flag what happens inside, remote workers may become involved, and the vehicle can pull over while police are summoned. Waymo’s system may have helped police recover an illegal firearm in this case. But the incident also raises a more basic question about what kind of space a robotaxi is: a ride with cameras for safety, a continuously monitored space, or a system that can call the cops on its own passengers. That question is already showing up in fiction. Robotaxis are making their debut as villains in Road Rage, an upcoming short film about a driverless car that turns against humans. One of the film’s more unsettling ideas is that a robotaxi could end up acting less like transportation and more like law enforcement. This month offered a glimpse of what that might look like.

articles.title: Judge orders Google to change ad auction rules
articles.summary: A federal judge has ordered Google to change its rules for auctioning online advertising on its platforms after finding last year that the search giant had an illegal monopoly over the technology connecting publishers and advertisers. The remedies were made public late Wednesday, when U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema unsealed her opinion from earlier this…
articles.body:
A federal judge has ordered Google to change its rules for auctioning online advertising on its platforms after finding last year that the search giant had an illegal monopoly over the technology connecting publishers and advertisers.

The remedies were made public late Wednesday, when U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema unsealed her opinion from earlier this month.

In the decision, Brinkema ruled that Google did not have to break up its ad tech business, rejecting the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) request to force the company to sell off its advertising exchange or open-source the technology behind its platform for publishers.

She accepted “most” of the behavioral remedies put forward by Google and the federal government, but the specifics remained under seal until Wednesday.

“The Court finds that structural remedies are neither realistic nor needed and that the parties’ substantially overlapping behavioral remedies as modified in this Memorandum Opinion will be sufficient to ‘effectively pry open to competition’ the ad tech markets,” Brinkema wrote in the opinion.

The judge suggested the DOJ’s rationale for a breakup “boils down to a lack of trust that Google will comply with an Order from this Court and an unrealistic desire for certainty.”

“Lack of trust alone or desire for ‘guaranteed certainty’ cannot justify divestiture,” she added.

However, Google will be barred from engaging in the behavior that ultimately prompted Brinkema to rule last April that it had improperly secured monopoly power over two markets involved in selling online ads.

Under the decision, the company will not be allowed to enforce policies tying its publisher-side platform, DoubleClick for Publishers (DFP), to its ad exchange platform, AdX.

The opinion also bars Google from reimplementing a series of functions that required publishers using DFP to give AdX special treatment on bids for ad space.

The firm is required to make both platforms interoperable with header bidding software, which allows publishers to offer up ad space to multiple ad exchanges before moving forward.

It also must make AdX interoperable with rival publisher-side platforms and provide publishers with data from both AdX and DFP.

Both platforms are barred from prioritizing Google’s own products, as is the company’s advertiser-side platform, AdWords.

Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward touted the ruling as “a significant victory for this Department’s efforts to protect and restore competition.”

“We will continue to review the opinion to consider the Department’s options,” he added in a statement. “Under President Trump’s and Attorney General Blanche’s leadership, we will never cease fighting for fair competition.”

It marks the second time that a judge has declined to break up Google’s products.

While U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta ruled in August 2024 that the company had an illegal monopoly over online search, he ultimately rejected the DOJ’s request to force Google to sell off its Chrome browser last September.

articles.title: Environment, health groups sue over Trump move to wipe out climate rules for power plants
articles.summary: Environmental and public health-focused organizations are suing the Trump administration over its move to wipe out most climate regulations on coal and gas power plants. The Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), American Lung Association, American Public Health Association, Clean Air Council, Clean Wisconsin and the Environmental Defense Fund filed the suit on Thursday. The move comes…
articles.body:
Environmental and public health-focused organizations are suing the Trump administration over its move to wipe out most climate regulations on coal and gas power plants.

The Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), American Lung Association, American Public Health Association, Clean Air Council, Clean Wisconsin and the Environmental Defense Fund filed the suit on Thursday.

The move comes just days after the administration finalized its move to gut the nation’s climate rules for coal and gas plants, eliminating the vast majority of rules that the Biden administration said would prevent 1.38 billion metric tons of carbon emissions through 2047, the equivalent of taking 328 million gas-powered cars off the road for a year.

That’s because existing coal and new gas plants will no longer have to prevent 90 percent of their carbon dioxide emissions from entering the atmosphere.

As the electric sector makes up a quarter of the U.S.’s total planet-heating emissions, that move could be one of the Trump administration’s most consequential climate rollbacks.

The administration estimated that it could save $310 billion.

The groups that sued Thursday said the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has a legal responsibility to limit planet-warming emissions, and that not doing so would have significant health consequences.

“Repealing these standards without a replacement is an abdication of EPA’s legal responsibility to protect public health and the environment,” said Meredith Hankins, federal climate legal director at NRDC, in a written statement. “The Clean Air Act and Supreme Court precedent demand that the EPA address climate pollution from the largest industrial source in the nation. The EPA’s legal reasoning is fatally flawed, so we are going to court.”

“Emissions from power plants drive climate change, and climate change is a health emergency,” said Harold Wimmer, president and CEO of the American Lung Association. “Measures that clean up power plant emissions also clean up other lung-harming pollutants at the same time. EPA has the authority and the responsibility to protect people’s health from air pollution.”

The EPA declined The Hill’s request for comment on the lawsuit. When it put forward the rule, the agency said that its move was a money saver.

“For over 15 years, the Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy. The Trump Administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin.

articles.title: Trump administration reduces protections for endangered species again
articles.summary: The Trump administration has further reduced protections for endangered species under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). That law prohibits any “take” of endangered species, which it defines as to “harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect, or to attempt to engage in any such conduct.” The administration recently repealed a previous definition of…
articles.body:
The Trump administration has further reduced protections for endangered species under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

That law prohibits any “take” of endangered species, which it defines as to “harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect, or to attempt to engage in any such conduct.”

The administration recently repealed a previous definition of prohibited “harm” under the law, now saying that in implementing that regulation, it will only consider an action “taking” a species if it is intentional.

“The Harm Rule rescinded the Services’ regulatory definitions of ‘harm,’ and adopted Justice [Antonin] Scalia’s interpretation of ‘take’ set out in the dissent in Babbitt v. Sweet Home Chapter of Communities for a Great Oregon,” the memo states.

“Under Justice Scalia’s interpretation, ‘take’ reaches only an affirmative act that is intentionally and purposefully directed at a particular animal,” it said.

The administration says, for example, that a ship that “inadvertently” strikes a whale “has not taken it,” and that felling a tree is not a take of bats residing in it.

The internal Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) memo was obtained and made public by the Center for Biological Diversity on Thursday.

Brett Hartl, the group’s government affairs director, said “Fish and Wildlife is going to effectively, I think, be entirely muzzled by this memo.”

“They are basically going to be told … ‘Look the other way on virtually all types of harmed or endangered species. We are not in the business of enforcing that anymore,'” he told The Hill.

The Interior Department, which oversees FWS, said via email that that the memo “accurately reflects the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s guidance for implementing the Endangered Species Act following the final rule rescinding the regulatory definition of ‘harm.'”

“Under the guidance, the ESA’s prohibition on ‘take’ continues to prohibit conduct including harassing, pursuing, hunting, shooting, wounding, killing, trapping, capturing or collecting protected wildlife,” said an unsigned statement from the department.

The move is the latest of multiple bites the Trump administration has taken out of the ESA. In July, it rolled back protections for at-risk animals considered “threatened,” a step below endangered.

articles.title: Human rights experts: ‘Reasonable grounds’ to believe US committed war crimes with Iran strikes
articles.summary: The United Nations’s fact-finding mission on Iran said Thursday it found “reasonable grounds” that the U.S. military committed war crimes in two airstrikes inside Iran and accused Iran’s government of carrying out crimes against humanity against its citizens during the forceful crackdown on anti-government protests earlier this year. The mission is made up of independent…
articles.body:
The United Nations’s fact-finding mission on Iran said Thursday it found “reasonable grounds” that the U.S. military committed war crimes in two airstrikes inside Iran and accused Iran’s government of carrying out crimes against humanity against its citizens during the forceful crackdown on anti-government protests earlier this year.

The mission is made up of independent experts and was established in November 2022 by the U.N.’s top human rights body, the Human Rights Council.

The Pentagon told The Hill it declines to comment on a report conducted by an outside organization, adding that the department’s investigation “remains ongoing” and “we have nothing to announce at the moment.”

In late February, at the start of the U.S. war against Iran, an all-girls school in the south of the country, Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School, was struck, killing nearly 160 people, including more than 120 schoolchildren.

The U.N. experts concluded in their report that the strike was a Tomahawk missile fired by the U.S. military on Feb. 28 at the school in Minab.

“The Mission considered the area of operations of the parties; its assessment of the origin and type of weapon used; several corroborated reports indicating that a preliminary U.S. military inquiry found U.S. forces responsible for the strike; the U.S. CENTCOM Commander’s assertion that the strike on the school ‘correlates’ with a U.S. strike; and the fact that the U.S. is the only party to the conflict that possesses Tomahawk missiles,” the group said in the 18-page report .

Top Trump administration officials have repeatedly said the U.S. military follows the laws of armed conflict and does not target civilians. Military officials have said for months that the Minab school strike is under investigation.

The mission also said a strike on a sports complex in Lamerd city, Fars Province, on Feb. 28, where more than 20 people were killed, was done by U.S. Central Command (Centcom) forces. Open-source analysis done by multiple news outlets found that the U.S.-made Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) was used in the airstrike.

Centcom said in March that U.S. forces did not fire missiles at Lamerd that day.

“The Mission notes key visual features of the PrSM’s silhouette identifiable in verified video, namely the long and sharp nose cone, smooth fuselage and short tail fins at the very base of the exhaust nozzle. It also observes that the missile detonations seen in verified videos occur directly above the target and not upon impact, which is consistent with a PrSM’s airburst’ mechanism,” the group said in the report.

The report also said Iran’s government carried out “violent repression” against anti-government protesters during late 2025 and early 2026 with widespread lethal forces that resulted in mass killings.

The killings by state security forces took place in all 31 provinces, with the highest death tolls reported in Karaj, Mashhad, Isfahan, Rasht and Tehran.

Security forces fired at protesters from rooftops. In Karaj, the regime forces fired tear gas to “trap demonstrators in narrow alleys before shooting them,” the report said, adding that at least 220 children were killed.

“Security forces also attacked healthcare facilities, beating and arresting wounded protestors and arresting some healthcare workers, which deterred victims from seeking life-saving care,” the experts said.

The mission “has strong grounds to believe” that the true number of those killed and injured is “significantly higher” than Iran’s government figures of 3,038 people killed and about 25,000 injured, which were presented in February.

“Iran has also used the death penalty against children in connection with the 2025/2026 protests, meaning individuals under the age of 18 at the time of the alleged offence,” the experts said in the report. “This is absolutely prohibited under international human rights law.”

articles.title: More people can get refunds from the FTC’s big settlement with Amazon.
articles.summary:
The September 2025 agreement said that Amazon would pay up to $1.5 billion over “deceptive” Prime signup practices. But after a court approved a joint motion, more people now qualify for refunds, there is now a maximum payment cap of $200 (up from $51), and Amazon will distribute refunds automatically, according to a press release.
[Link: FTC Announces Additional Payments to Consumers Stemming from FTC’s Amazon Prime Settlement | https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/09/ftc-announces-additional-payments-consumers-stemming-ftcs-amazon-prime-settlement | Federal Trade Commission]
